voiceover.text: So, why does a program stop working? Someone joins a gym and does exactly the same session, with exactly the same weights, three times a week. For two months they get noticeably stronger. For the next four, they get no stronger at all, and they never miss a session. Write down why the first two months worked and the next four didn't. Then write the smallest change you'd make.

scenes.title: progressive overload, and its two failure modes

voiceover.text: The body adapts to a stress it isn't used to. That change is adaptation. Once it's adapted, the same stress isn't new any more, so it stops driving change. That's the hook. The load was new for two months, then it wasn't. So the load has to rise, which is progressive overload. But it has to rise slowly enough to recover, because adaptation happens during recovery, not during the session. So the principle has two failure modes. Too little progression gives a plateau. Too much gives overtraining: fatigue builds faster than recovery, performance falls, and injury or illness follow. And here's the trap. On the way up, overtraining looks like the best progress of all, until it collapses.

scenes.title: the variables of overload, one at a time

voiceover.text: In Year 11 you met FITT: frequency, intensity, time and type. Each one is a way to progress. In aerobic training, that's more sessions, a faster pace, longer runs, or moving from continuous to intervals. In strength training, it's more sessions per muscle, a heavier load, more reps and sets, or moving from a machine to free weights. Aerobic overload usually rises through volume, and a common guide is about ten per cent a week. Strength overload usually rises through load, once the target reps are done with good technique. And change one variable at a time. If load, volume and frequency all rise in the same week and the athlete breaks down, you can't tell which change did it. So the smallest change for our gym-goer is a small load increase once the reps feel solid.

Overload says how much more. A training threshold says more than what: the minimum intensity that produces a training effect for a system. In aerobic training, you met the two thresholds earlier. Below about seventy per cent of maximum heart rate, the stimulus usually becomes too small to keep improving aerobic fitness. Above the lactate threshold, by-products build up and the work can't last. Strength has thresholds too, in per cent of one-rep max, the heaviest load you can lift once. Below about sixty-five per cent you mostly build endurance. For maximal strength in trained lifters, it's about eighty-five per cent. Beginners get stronger on much lighter loads, because their threshold is lower. Same idea, different units.

Thresholds belong to the athlete, and they move. The same eight-kilometre jog is training for a beginner and recovery for a trained runner. And a threshold is a floor for one adaptation, not for all benefit. Easy work still helps recovery and health.

Specificity means the body adapts to the exact stress you apply, so training should match the sport. The marks come from naming which way a session matches or misses. Five questions. Energy system: does it stress the system the event uses? A hundred-metre sprinter doing only long runs fails that. Movement pattern: does the exercise look like the sport's action? A cyclist training only on a seated leg machine misses that. Speed: is it done at the sport's velocity? A jumper doing only heavy, slow lifts gets stronger, but not quicker off the ground. And context: are the decision and the pressure there? But total specificity has a cost: little variety, weaknesses left unfixed, and the same tissue loaded again and again, which is how overuse injuries start. So say which dimension, not just "not specific".

scenes.title: applying them to aerobic and strength training, and evaluating

voiceover.text: The dot point asks you to evaluate how these apply to aerobic and strength training. They apply validly to both, but with different precision. In strength training, load, reps and sets are countable, so overload can be set exactly. In aerobic training, intensity is read from heart rate or effort, and heat, sleep, illness and hydration all shift it, so the same prescription gives a different stimulus on different days. To evaluate a program, use four steps: name the principle, quote the feature that shows it, predict the consequence, and recommend a change. A lifter adds ten kilograms to every lift every week. That's overload breached at the top: technique fails, fatigue builds, injury risk rises. Recommend small steps, only once the reps are solid.
Two things to remember. Too little is a plateau, too much is a breakdown. And thresholds belong to the athlete, not the activity.

Two exam questions. First. A tennis player's conditioning is all straight-line running. A swimmer doubles their weekly distance in one week, changing nothing else. For each, name the principle breached, quote the feature that shows it, and predict the consequence. Pause here to answer.

The tennis player breaches specificity, in movement pattern: tennis moves sideways and changes direction, so court movement won't improve. The swimmer breaches progressive overload: one variable, but doubled, far past a ten per cent step, so fatigue outruns recovery and injury risk rises. The classic mistake is saying "not specific" without the dimension.

scenes.title: attempt two (the walk that got easy)

voiceover.text: Second. A previously inactive adult walks twenty minutes a day at a pace that lifts their heart rate to seventy-five per cent of maximum heart rate. After four months, the same walk only reaches sixty per cent of maximum heart rate. Using training thresholds, explain what has happened, and recommend a change. Pause here to answer.

They've adapted, so the same walk is now easier for their heart. At sixty per cent, it's below the aerobic training zone, so it keeps health benefits but drives little new aerobic adaptation. Progress it: walk faster, add hills or intervals, or go longer. The classic mistake is calling the walk useless.

So keep raising the load, a little at a time, keep it above the right threshold for that athlete, and match it to the sport, dimension by dimension. But what if the training stops altogether, for injury, illness or the off-season? Does the staircase just stay where it is? What happens when training stops?
